claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 can be processed to exhibit a hierarchical heterostructure containing distinct phases, interfaces, and refined precipitate distributions.
Grain-size distribution mediates the transition from elastic deformation through yielding to fracture initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Interphase boundaries mediate strength, ductility, and fracture-related behavior in this class of alloy.
Precipitate size and distribution mediate the transition from elastic deformation through yielding to fracture initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Direct microstructural inputs allow the proposed simulation to capture elastic response more accurately and efficiently.
Direct microstructural inputs allow the proposed simulation to capture dislocation nucleation.
Direct microstructural inputs allow the proposed simulation to capture crack propagation.
Machine-learning models trained on limited experimental data can rapidly update property predictions.
Machine learning reduces the computational detail required relative to full-scale finite-element or molecular-dynamics simulations.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus within approximately 10–15% of experimental measurements.
The proposed model will predict yield strength within approximately 10–15% of experimental measurements.
The proposed model will predict fracture-related behavior within approximately 10–15% of experimental measurements.
The proposed model will reduce computational time by at least 50% relative to traditional simulation methods.
Conventional full-scale finite-element or atomistic simulations are computationally intensive.
Conventional simulations often deviate more from measured tensile and fracture properties than the proposed approach.
The HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure remains sufficiently stable during quasi-static testing from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Dynamic microstructural evolution at high strain rates or extreme temperatures may cause the proposed model to fail.
Failure to include descriptors for operative deformation mechanisms may reduce predictive accuracy.
Predictive improvement depends on the quality of microstructural inputs and the representativeness of the machine-learning training set.
Unaccounted microstructural evolution or rare defect interactions could reduce predictive accuracy.
